claims.text: Mupirocin or retapamulin twice daily for 5 days for bullous and nonbullous impetigo (mild bullous can be treated topically)
claims.quote: Treatment of bullous and nonbullous impetigo should be with either mupirocin or retapamulin twice daily (bid) for 5 days (strong, high).

claims.text: Bullous and nonbullous impetigo can be treated topically or orally; oral therapy for numerous lesions or outbreaks
claims.quote: Bullous and nonbullous impetigo can be treated with oral or topical antimicrobials, but oral therapy is recommended for patients with numerous lesions or in outbreaks affecting several people

claims.text: Oral course is a 7-day regimen active against S. aureus
claims.quote: Oral therapy for ecthyma or impetigo should be a 7-day regimen with an agent active against S. aureus

claims.text: Dicloxacillin or cephalexin because impetigo staph is usually methicillin susceptible; most impetigo staph is not MRSA
claims.quote: Because S. aureus isolates from impetigo and ecthyma are usually methicillin susceptible, dicloxacillin or cephalexin is recommended.

claims.text: Doxycycline, clindamycin, or TMP-SMX when MRSA suspected or confirmed
claims.quote: When MRSA is suspected or confirmed, doxycycline, clindamycin, or sulfamethoxazole-trimethoprim (SMX-TMP) is recommended

claims.text: Ecthyma should be treated with an oral antibiotic
claims.quote: Treatment for ecthyma should be an oral antimicrobial.

claims.text: Table: impetigo treated with topical or oral antibiotics
claims.quote: Bullous and nonbullous impetigo can be treated with oral or topical antimicrobials

claims.text: Topical antibiotics cured more people than placebo
claims.quote: Topical antibiotic treatment showed better cure rates than placebo (pooled risk ratio (RR) 2. 24, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.61 to 3.13) in 6 studies with 575 participants.

claims.text: Topical mupirocin and fusidic acid as effective as or more effective than oral antibiotics; unclear for extensive impetigo
claims.quote: There is good evidence that topical mupirocin and topical fusidic acid are equally, or more, effective than oral treatment. Due to the lack of studies in people with extensive impetigo, it is unclear if oral antibiotics are superior

claims.text: Little evidence for disinfectants; topical antibiotics better than disinfecting treatments
claims.quote: There was a lack of evidence for the benefit of using disinfectant solutions. When 2 studies with 292 participants were pooled, topical antibiotics were significantly better than disinfecting treatments

claims.text: Most common in children 2 to 5; more than 3 million U.S. cases a year
claims.quote: Impetigo is a superficial skin infection that most commonly affects children 2 to 5 years of age. In the United States, more than 3 million cases of impetigo occur annually.

claims.text: Nonbullous about 70 percent, bullous about 30 percent; caused by group A strep and S. aureus
claims.quote: Impetigo can be nonbullous (70%) or bullous (30%) and is most commonly caused by group A streptococcus and Staphylococcus aureus.

claims.text: Clinical diagnosis; culture considered for treatment failure, recurrence, or uncertainty
claims.quote: Cultures of impetigo lesions should be considered in cases of inadequate response to therapy, recurrence, or diagnostic uncertainty.

claims.text: Papules progress to ruptured blisters over 4 to 6 days with honey-colored crusts; suspect impetigo
claims.quote: should be suspected in individuals with erythematous papules that progress to ruptured vesicles or bullae over 4 to 6 days, forming honey-colored crusts.

claims.text: Risk factors: skin barrier disruption, poor hygiene, crowding, hot humid climates, malnutrition, diabetes
claims.quote: Risk factors for impetigo include disruptions to the skin barrier, poor hygiene, crowded living environments, living in hot and humid climates, malnutrition, and diabetes.

claims.text: Mupirocin 2% or retapamulin 1% first for mild nonbullous and bullous impetigo
claims.quote: Topical mupirocin 2% ointment or retapamulin 1% ointment are the recommended initial treatments for mild, nonbullous and bullous impetigo.

claims.text: Oral dicloxacillin or cephalexin targeting strep and S. aureus for outbreaks or severe multilesional disease not responding in 3 to 5 days
claims.quote: Oral antibiotics, such as dicloxacillin or cephalexin, should be targeted to group A streptococci and S. aureus and are recommended for outbreaks to decrease infection transmission or for severe, multilesional disease that does not respond to topical therapy within 3 to 5 days.

claims.text: Return 12 to 24 hours after starting antibiotics or on clinical improvement; hand hygiene and washing objects reduce spread and recurrence
claims.quote: Reducing the spread and recurrence of impetigo includes good hand hygiene, thoroughly washing objects used by people with impetigo, and refraining from returning to work or school until 12 to 24 hours after initiating antibiotic treatment or clinical improvement occurs.

claims.text: Ozenoxacin FDA approved 2017, discontinued in the US as of September 2025
claims.quote: approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in 2017 for the treatment of impetigo; however, it has been discontinued in the United States as of September 2025 and is expensive.

references.cited_as: Trang DT, Buck EC, Schoenherr DT. Impetigo: Rapid Evidence Review. American Family Physician. 2026;113(2):175-180. PMID 41839109. aafp.org

claims.text: Caused by group A strep, S. aureus, or both
claims.quote: Impetigo is a skin infection caused by bacteria: either group A Streptococcus, Staphylococcus aureus, or both.

claims.text: Red, itchy sores that break open, leak fluid or pus, form honey-colored scab
claims.quote: Symptoms include red, itchy sores that break open and leak a clear fluid or pus for a few days.

claims.text: Crusty yellow or honey-colored scab; heals without scarring
claims.quote: Next, a crusty yellow or "honey-colored" scab forms over the sore, which then heals without leaving a scar.

claims.text: Exposed skin; arms, legs, mouth, nose
claims.quote: The sores can occur anywhere on the body but most often affect exposed skin.

claims.text: Incubation about 10 days for group A strep
claims.quote: It usually takes 10 days for sores to appear after someone is exposed to group A strep bacteria.

claims.text: Bacteria often spread to household members
claims.quote: For example, if someone has impetigo, the bacteria often spread to other people in their household.

claims.text: Crowded settings: daycare and schools, detention facilities, shelters, military training
claims.quote: Crowded conditions can increase the risk of spreading impetigo. These settings include: Daycare centers and schools Detention or correctional facilities Homeless shelters Military training facilities

claims.text: Return to work or school after starting antibiotics with sores covered
claims.quote: People with impetigo can return to work, school, or daycare if they have started antibiotic treatment. They should also cover all sores on exposed skin.

claims.text: Complications rare, include PSGN
claims.quote: Very rarely, complications can include post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis and rheumatic fever.

references.notes: Book chapter, no PMID/DOI. Authors per the chapter disclosures and the AFP 2026 reference list (Nardi NM, Schaefer TJ). Tertiary source. It states systemic antibiotics for all bullous impetigo, which conflicts with IDSA 2014 and AFP 2026 (topical for mild bullous); the guide follows the guidelines and names the disagreement.
